# Background
## Literature Review

Urban water infrastructure in the United States is aging, underfunded, and
increasingly recognized as a site of environmental injustice. Erban and
Walker's [-@erban2019] systems analysis of Chicago's water infrastructure
provides essential context for understanding the region's challenges: the
city's Department of Water Management (DWM) supplies not only Chicago but
125 suburban municipalities with water drawn from Lake Michigan, connecting
suburban Cook County's water security directly to the city's own
infrastructure decisions and financial health [@erban2019]. Their analysis
shows that DWM revenues—drawn almost entirely from water and sewer fees—have
increasingly been diverted to non-water municipal obligations, including
pension deficits, even as capital investment needs (such as lead service
line replacement) remain substantial [@erban2019]. This entanglement of
"Enterprise" water revenues with general municipal finance, combined with
documented cases of suburbs falling into arrears on water payments to the
city [@erban2019], illustrates a structural funding vulnerability that
likely compounds the difficulty of remediating lead infrastructure in
lower-income suburban systems that lack independent capital capacity.

This funding vulnerability is now operating within a newly tightened
regulatory environment. Illinois's Lead Service Line Replacement and
Notification Act, codified at 415 ILCS 5/17.12 and effective January 1,
2022, mandates that every community water supply in the state—including
suburban Cook County municipalities—fully replace all lead service lines,
with no partial replacements permitted except for a narrow class of
very high-volume utilities [@illinois2021]. The Act imposes a phased
compliance structure: municipalities were required to submit initial and
updated service line inventories between 2022 and 2024, and must submit
replacement plans culminating in a final comprehensive plan due April 15,
2027, after which statutory replacement deadlines are scaled to the number
of lead lines a system reports, in practice extending compliance for
larger systems by decades [@illinois2021]. Because the Act funds
replacement in part through a fee assessed on billed water usage collected
by the community water supplies themselves, and routes broader support
through the state-administered Lead Service Line Replacement Fund
[@illinois2021], smaller or lower-income suburban systems—those Balazs and
Ray [-@balazs2014] identify as constrained by low technical, managerial,
and financial (TMF) capacity—may struggle both to generate adequate local
fee revenue and to compete for state funds requiring the very
administrative capacity they lack. This tension is sharpened by the
federal Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI), finalized by EPA in
October 2024 [@epa2024lcri], which generally requires replacement within 10 years—a
substantially shorter window than Illinois's own statutory timeline
permits for many systems [@illinois2021]. For suburban Cook County water
agencies serving economically challenged populations, this means the more
protective federal deadline, rather than the more forgiving state
schedule, is likely to function as the binding constraint, even as these
same agencies face the structural revenue diversion pressures documented
by Erban and Walker [-@erban2019].

The broader environmental justice literature helps explain why such
infrastructural vulnerabilities disproportionately burden economically
challenged communities. Balazs and Ray's [-@balazs2014] Drinking Water
Disparities Framework, though developed in the context of California's San
Joaquin Valley, offers a transferable analytic structure: natural, built,
and sociopolitical factors interact across state, county, community, and
household levels to produce and sustain unequal exposure to contaminated
water [@balazs2014]. Central to their framework is the finding that small
or under-resourced water systems face compounding barriers—not only
inadequate infrastructure but also low TMF capacity—that make securing
remediation funding especially difficult, since state and federal funding
criteria often require the very capacity that disadvantaged systems lack
[@balazs2014]. This dynamic is directly relevant to suburban Cook County,
where smaller municipal or mixed public-private systems serving
lower-income populations may be structurally less equipped to pursue lead
service line replacement funding—whether through Illinois's own Lead
Service Line Replacement Fund or federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law
channels—than wealthier, better-staffed suburban utilities.

Karasaki et al.'s [-@karasaki2023] critical review of primary-data
environmental justice studies on drinking water reinforces this picture
while highlighting a persistent research gap: most studies document
*distributive* injustice (disparities in water quality or infrastructure
access) and, to a lesser extent, *procedural* injustice (exclusion from
decision-making), but few explicitly measure the corrective or remediation
process itself [@karasaki2023]. Their review also underscores that
infrastructural disconnection and legacy contamination problems—including
lead—are concentrated in unincorporated, low-income, and minority
communities, and that the state's role in redress is contested, since
state and municipal actors are often implicated in the very
underinvestment that produced the hazard [@karasaki2023]. Williamson et
al.'s [-@williamson2020] scoping review of environmental justice
capacity-building complements this by showing that even where
community-academic partnerships and community organizing succeed in
raising awareness and building citizen participation, translation into
actual policy, system, or environmental (PSE) change—such as pipe
replacement—occurs in only a minority of cases [@williamson2020],
suggesting that community mobilization alone is insufficient without
dedicated public investment, and that statutory mandates such as 415
ILCS 5/17.12 may be a necessary, if not sufficient, condition for
remediation in disadvantaged suburban systems.

Finally, Fanaian et al.'s [-@fanaian2025] systematic review of the broader
"water justice" literature situates these local dynamics within an
evolving theoretical landscape, noting a shift from earlier
distributive/procedural framings toward attention to structural power
imbalances, institutional capture, and the limits of purely technical or
infrastructural "fixes" [@fanaian2025]. Their review is explicit that
infrastructure-led solutions—desalination, pipe replacement, treatment
upgrades—cannot be treated as stand-alone remedies, since without
accompanying institutional reform and sustained funding accountability,
gains toward water justice are frequently reversed by shifts in political
leadership or budget priorities [@fanaian2025]. Taken together, this
literature suggests that lead pipe remediation in economically challenged
suburban Cook County communities is unlikely to be resolved through
statutory mandate or infrastructure spending alone; it will require
addressing the underlying financial entanglement of water utility revenue
with municipal budgets, the TMF capacity gaps of smaller systems, and
sustained, redistributive funding mechanisms responsive to structural
inequity rather than reliant on individual communities' capacity to
advocate for themselves or comply unassisted with Illinois's phased
statutory deadlines.

# Methodology

## Public Water System Service Area Boundaries

As an initial step in mapping jurisdictional responsibility for drinking water in suburban Cook County, service area boundaries were obtained from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Public Water System Service Area Boundaries dataset (Version 3, released March 2026) [@epa2026pwsboundaries]. This national geospatial dataset combines service area boundaries published by state agencies and individual water systems with EPA-modeled boundaries generated for systems where authoritative state data was unavailable. The dataset covers over 44,000 community water systems nationally, representing approximately 99% of the population served by community water systems in the United States, and additionally maps transient and non-transient non-community water systems (e.g., schools, workplaces, and other facilities with their own water supply) at the parcel level.

Each mapped service area is linked to its system's federal Public Water System Identification number (PWSID), enabling direct integration with compliance and violation records maintained in the EPA's Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS) [@epaecho2026]. This linkage allows regulatory compliance history to be layered spatially onto jurisdictional boundaries, supporting analysis of whether violations cluster within particular governance types or geographic areas of suburban Cook County.

Boundaries were retrieved programmatically via the dataset's ArcGIS REST Feature Service and clipped to a Cook County study area boundary drawn from the U.S. Census Bureau's cartographic boundary files [@uscensus2023counties]. Because the dataset combines authoritative and EPA-modeled boundaries, systems were flagged by boundary source (state/utility-sourced vs. EPA-modeled) to account for potential differences in spatial accuracy across the study area; this distinction is reported where relevant to interpretation of findings.

```{r}
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Download EPA Public Water System (Community Water System) Service Area
## Boundaries for Cook County, IL from the national ArcGIS FeatureServer
##
## Source: EPA Office of Water, Public Water System Service Area Boundaries v3
## https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/public-water-system-service-areas
## REST endpoint:
## https://services.arcgis.com/cJ9YHowT8TU7DUyn/arcgis/rest/services/Water_System_Boundaries/FeatureServer
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

## ---- 0. Setup ---------------------------------------------------------------

## IMPORTANT: EPA's Public Water System Service Area Boundaries dataset
## includes some invalid polygons (self-intersections, duplicate vertices),
## especially among EPA-modeled boundaries. sf's default spherical geometry
## engine (s2) is strict about validity and will throw an error like:
##   "Loop 2 is not valid: Edge 1694 has duplicate vertex with edge 1731"
## Turning off s2 (falls back to the more forgiving GEOS planar engine) avoids
## this at the query/filter stage. Geometries are still explicitly repaired
## with st_make_valid() below as a second safeguard.
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

feature_server_url <- "https://services.arcgis.com/cJ9YHowT8TU7DUyn/arcgis/rest/services/Water_System_Boundaries/FeatureServer"

## ---- 1. Get a Cook County, IL boundary to use as a spatial filter -----------
## This avoids downloading the entire national dataset (44,000+ systems).

cook_county <- counties(state = "IL", cb = TRUE, year = 2023) |>
  filter(NAME == "Cook") |>
  st_transform(4326)

## ---- 2. PREFERRED METHOD: arcgislayers package -----------------------------
## arcgislayers (R-ArcGIS team) handles pagination, field selection, and
## spatial filtering automatically -- it is the modern, maintained way to
## pull data from an Esri FeatureServer/MapServer into R as an sf object.

if (!requireNamespace("arcgislayers", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("arcgislayers", repos = c("https://r-arcgis.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
}

# List the layers/sublayers on this FeatureServer so you can confirm the
# correct layer index (there may be more than one, e.g. active vs. historical).
service <- arc_open(feature_server_url)
print(service)  # inspect layer names/IDs in the console

# Typically layer 0 is the main community water system boundaries layer --
# adjust the index below if arc_open() shows otherwise.
cws_layer <- arc_open(paste0(feature_server_url, "/0"))

# Pull only features that intersect the Cook County boundary, and only the
# columns we care about, to keep the request lean.
cook_cws_raw <- arc_select(
  cws_layer,
  filter_geom = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(cook_county)),  # bounding-box prefilter
  fields = NULL  # NULL = all fields; replace with a character vector to limit
)

# Repair invalid geometries (self-intersections, duplicate vertices) before
# doing any further spatial operations -- this is what the s2 error flagged.
cook_cws_valid <- cook_cws_raw |>
  st_make_valid()

# Confirm nothing is still invalid; report count of any remaining problem rows
n_invalid <- sum(!st_is_valid(cook_cws_valid))
if (n_invalid > 0) {
  message(n_invalid, " feature(s) remain invalid after st_make_valid(); ",
          "these will be dropped before clipping.")
  cook_cws_valid <- cook_cws_valid[st_is_valid(cook_cws_valid), ]
}

cook_cws <- cook_cws_valid |>
  st_filter(cook_county, .predicate = st_intersects)  # precise clip to county polygon

## ---- 3. FALLBACK METHOD: manual REST query with pagination -----------------
## Use this if arcgislayers is unavailable/fails (e.g. restricted network).
## Esri REST services usually cap each response at ~1,000-2,000 records
## (maxRecordCount), so we page through results with resultOffset.

fallback_download <- function(base_url, layer_id = 0, where = "1=1",
                               geometry_sf = NULL, batch_size = 1000) {
  library(httr2)
  library(geojsonsf)

  query_url <- paste0(base_url, "/", layer_id, "/query")

  # Build an ArcGIS JSON envelope from the sf bbox, if a filter geometry is given
  geom_param <- NULL
  if (!is.null(geometry_sf)) {
    bb <- st_bbox(st_transform(geometry_sf, 4326))
    geom_param <- sprintf(
      '{"xmin":%f,"ymin":%f,"xmax":%f,"ymax":%f,"spatialReference":{"wkid":4326}}',
      bb["xmin"], bb["ymin"], bb["xmax"], bb["ymax"]
    )
  }

  all_features <- list()
  offset <- 0
  repeat {
    req <- request(query_url) |>
      req_url_query(
        where = where,
        outFields = "*",
        f = "geojson",
        resultOffset = offset,
        resultRecordCount = batch_size,
        geometry = geom_param,
        geometryType = if (!is.null(geom_param)) "esriGeometryEnvelope" else NULL,
        inSR = if (!is.null(geom_param)) 4326 else NULL,
        spatialRel = if (!is.null(geom_param)) "esriSpatialRelIntersects" else NULL
      )

    resp <- req_perform(req)
    txt <- resp_body_string(resp)

    batch_sf <- geojson_sf(txt)
    if (nrow(batch_sf) == 0) break

    all_features[[length(all_features) + 1]] <- batch_sf
    if (nrow(batch_sf) < batch_size) break
    offset <- offset + batch_size
  }

  dplyr::bind_rows(all_features) |>
    st_as_sf() |>
    st_make_valid()  # same fix as the primary method -- repairs invalid EPA geometries
}

# Uncomment to use the fallback instead of arcgislayers:
# cook_cws <- fallback_download(
#   base_url     = feature_server_url,
#   layer_id     = 0,
#   geometry_sf  = cook_county
# ) |>
#   st_filter(cook_county, .predicate = st_intersects)

## ---- 4. Inspect and save -----------------------------------------------------

glimpse(st_drop_geometry(cook_cws))

# Save as a GeoPackage (preferred - single file, preserves types) and Shapefile
# (for compatibility with older GIS software) into /mnt/user-data/outputs
st_write(cook_cws, "data/spatial/cook_county_water_system_boundaries.gpkg",
          delete_dsn = TRUE)
st_write(cook_cws, "data/spatial/cook_county_water_system_boundaries.shp",
          delete_dsn = TRUE)

## ---- 5. Quick visual check ----------------------------------------------------

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = cook_county, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(data = cook_cws, aes(fill = PWS_Name), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1,
          show.legend = FALSE, alpha = 0.85) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Community Water System Service Areas, Cook County, IL",
    caption = "Source: U.S. EPA Public Water System Service Area Boundaries (v3)"
  )

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## NOTES
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
##   EPA data dictionary for the authoritative field list:
##   https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-03/data-dictionary_v3_03162026.pdf
##
## - This layer covers COMMUNITY water systems only. Non-community systems
##   (schools, gas stations, small transient supplies) are in a separate
##   FeatureServer -- see the EPA page for that endpoint if needed.
##
## - The boundary data mixes EPA-modeled boundaries with authoritative
##   state/utility-sourced boundaries. Check the SOURCE or DATA_SRC field
##   (naming varies by version) to flag which Cook County systems are
##   modeled estimates vs. verified boundaries -- worth reporting in your
##   methods section.
##
## - To link to SDWIS violation data, join on the PWSID field to EPA's
##   ECHO/SDWIS downloads: https://echo.epa.gov/tools/data-downloads/sdwa-download-summary
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

## Drinking Water Violation and Compliance

Water quality violation and enforcement data were obtained from the U.S. EPA's Enforcement and Compliance History Online (ECHO) system, which incorporates records from the Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS) [@epaecho2026]. SDWIS contains system-level monitoring, violation, and enforcement data reported by states to EPA under the Safe Drinking Water Act, refreshed quarterly. Data were retrieved via ECHO's bulk SDWA download, which was filtered to public water systems with an Illinois-prefixed system identifier (PWSID), then further narrowed to systems identified as serving Cook County based on the county-served field in SDWIS's geographic area records.

Because this county designation is self-reported by states and water systems and may be incomplete for some systems, this attribution was cross-checked against a spatial join of PWSID-linked service area boundaries (see prior section) to the Cook County geographic boundary; discrepancies between the two methods were retained and reported rather than reconciled, to avoid understating potential gaps in system-level geographic reporting.

Violation records were joined to system-level identifying information—including ownership type (local government, private, public/private, state, or federal), population served, and primary water source—to support analysis of whether violation patterns differ by governance structure. Violation and contaminant codes were decoded into descriptive labels using SDWIS's reference code table. Violations specific to the Lead and Copper Rule were identified separately to align with this study's focus on lead service line infrastructure, and corresponding lead and copper sample measurement data were retrieved to supplement binary violation status with underlying concentration data where available.

For each system, violations were summarized by total count, count of health-based violations, count of unresolved violations (i.e., violations not yet subject to a resolving enforcement action, per EPA's compliance status categories), and count of Lead and Copper Rule violations specifically. This system-level summary was structured for direct linkage, via PWSID, to the water system service area boundaries described above, enabling spatial analysis of violation patterns across suburban Cook County's jurisdictional landscape.

It should be noted that the retrieved dataset reflects a single quarterly snapshot rather than a longitudinal violation history; analyses of trends over time would require supplementary retrieval of historical SDWIS data.
```{r}
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Download and process SDWIS violation/compliance data (via EPA's ECHO
## bulk download) for Illinois public water systems, and join to the
## Cook County water system service area boundaries pulled previously.
##
## Source: EPA ECHO - Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) Data Downloads
## Summary/data dictionary: https://echo.epa.gov/tools/data-downloads/sdwa-download-summary
## Bulk download index:     https://echo.epa.gov/files/echodownloads/
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

## ---- 0. Setup ----------------------------------------------------------------

# Install once if needed:
# install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "purrr", "stringr", "sf"))

data_dir <- "data/tabular"
dir.create(data_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

zip_url  <- "https://echo.epa.gov/files/echodownloads/SDWA_latest_downloads.zip"
zip_path <- file.path(data_dir, "SDWA_latest_downloads.zip")

## ---- 1. Download the bulk SDWA dataset ---------------------------------------
## NOTE: This is a large file (~400+ MB) containing every public water system
## nationally. EPA refreshes it quarterly. Rather than paginating a REST API
## (as with the boundary data), the SDWIS/ECHO data is distributed as a single
## bulk ZIP of CSVs, which is the intended and far more efficient access
## method for this dataset.

if (!file.exists(zip_path)) {
  download.file(zip_url, destfile = zip_path, mode = "wb")
}

## ---- 2. Extract only the files we need ---------------------------------------
## The ZIP contains ~10 CSVs (see the SDWA Data Download Summary for the full
## file list/dictionary). We only need a subset for a jurisdiction/compliance
## analysis: the system inventory, violations & enforcement, service areas,
## geographic areas (for county name), and the reference code table (to
## decode violation/contaminant codes into readable labels).

needed_files <- c(
  "SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS.csv",
  "SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT.csv",
  "SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv",
  "SDWA_SERVICE_AREAS.csv",
  "SDWA_REF_CODE_VALUES.csv",
  "SDWA_LCR_SAMPLES.csv"          # Lead & Copper Rule sample data
)

zip_contents <- unzip("data/tabular/SDWA_latest_downloads.zip", list = TRUE)$Name

# Match needed files case-insensitively in case EPA changes casing between
# quarterly releases
files_to_extract <- zip_contents[
  toupper(zip_contents) %in% toupper(needed_files)
]

missing <- setdiff(toupper(needed_files), toupper(files_to_extract))
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  message("Note: the following expected files were not found in this quarter's ZIP: ",
          paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
          "\nCheck zip_contents (printed below) for the current file list/naming.")
  print(zip_contents)
}

unzip(zip_path, files = files_to_extract, exdir = data_dir, overwrite = TRUE)

## ---- 3. Read in and filter to Illinois -----------------------------------
## PWSID's first two characters are the state/region code (e.g., "IL"), so we
## can filter every table to Illinois systems before any join, which keeps
## the working data small.

read_il <- function(filename) {
  path <- file.path(data_dir, filename)
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  read_csv(path, guess_max = 100000, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    filter(str_starts(PWSID, "IL"))
}

pws        <- read_il("SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS.csv")
violations <- read_il("SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT.csv")
geo_areas  <- read_il("SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv")
svc_areas  <- read_il("SDWA_SERVICE_AREAS.csv")
lcr_samples <- read_il("SDWA_LCR_SAMPLES.csv")

# Reference codes are not state-specific -- read in full (it's a small file)
ref_codes <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "SDWA_REF_CODE_VALUES.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)

## ---- 4. Narrow to Cook County systems -----------------------------------------
## SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv includes a COUNTY_SERVED field, which is the most
## direct way to identify Cook County systems within the Illinois subset.
## This is self-reported by water systems/states and may be incomplete for
## some systems -- cross-check counts against the boundary-based approach
## (spatial join to the Cook County polygon from the previous script) to
## catch systems missing a county label.

cook_pwsids <- geo_areas |>
  filter(str_to_upper(COUNTY_SERVED) == "COOK") |>
  distinct(PWSID) |>
  pull(PWSID)

message(length(cook_pwsids), " unique PWSIDs identified as serving Cook County ",
        "via the COUNTY_SERVED field.")

pws_cook        <- pws        |> filter(PWSID %in% cook_pwsids)
violations_cook <- violations |> filter(PWSID %in% cook_pwsids)
lcr_cook        <- lcr_samples |> filter(PWSID %in% cook_pwsids)

## ---- 5. Decode key coded fields using the reference table --------------------

decode <- function(df, code_col, value_type, new_col) {
  lookup <- ref_codes |>
    filter(VALUE_TYPE == value_type) |>
    select(VALUE_CODE, VALUE_DESCRIPTION) |>
    rename(!!new_col := VALUE_DESCRIPTION)

  df |>
    left_join(lookup, by = setNames("VALUE_CODE", code_col))
}

violations_cook <- violations_cook |>
  decode("VIOLATION_CODE", "VIOLATION_CODE", "violation_description") |>
  decode("CONTAMINANT_CODE", "CONTAMINANT_CODE", "contaminant_description")

## ---- 6. Summarize violations by system (a natural first analytic table) ------

## VIOL_LAST_REPORTED_DATE is character (MM/DD/YYYY); convert to Date before
## taking the max so the most recent date is found chronologically, not
## alphabetically. Also add the year of the most recent violation.
violation_summary <- violations_cook |>
  mutate(viol_last_reported_date = coalesce(
    as.Date(VIOL_LAST_REPORTED_DATE, format = "%m/%d/%Y"),
    as.Date(VIOL_LAST_REPORTED_DATE, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
  )) |>
  group_by(PWSID) |>
  summarise(
    n_violations           = n(),
    n_health_based         = sum(IS_HEALTH_BASED_IND == "Y", na.rm = TRUE),
    n_unresolved           = sum(VIOLATION_STATUS %in% c("Unaddressed", "Addressed"), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_lead_copper_rule     = sum(RULE_CODE == "350", na.rm = TRUE),
    most_recent_violation  = if (all(is.na(viol_last_reported_date))) as.Date(NA)
                             else max(viol_last_reported_date, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(most_recent_violation_year = as.numeric(format(most_recent_violation, "%Y")))

pws_cook_summary <- pws_cook |>
  select(PWSID, PWS_NAME, OWNER_TYPE_CODE, POPULATION_SERVED_COUNT,
         PRIMARY_SOURCE_CODE, PWS_ACTIVITY_CODE, SERVICE_CONNECTIONS_COUNT) |>
  left_join(violation_summary, by = "PWSID") |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("n_"), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)))

## ---- 7. Save outputs ------------------------------------------------------

out_dir <- "/mnt/user-data/outputs"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

write_csv(pws_cook,          file.path(out_dir, "cook_county_pws_inventory.csv"))
write_csv(violations_cook,   file.path(out_dir, "cook_county_sdwa_violations.csv"))
write_csv(lcr_cook,          file.path(out_dir, "cook_county_lead_copper_samples.csv"))
write_csv(pws_cook_summary,  file.path(out_dir, "cook_county_pws_violation_summary.csv"))

## ---- 8. (Optional) Join to the service area boundaries from the prior script --
## If cook_cws (the sf object from download_water_system_boundaries.R) is
## already loaded in this session, join the violation summary directly onto
## the spatial boundaries on PWSID for mapping.

library(sf)
cook_cws_with_violations <- cook_cws |>
  left_join(pws_cook_summary, by = c("PWSID" = "PWSID"))

st_write(cook_cws_with_violations,
          file.path("data/spatial/cook_county_water_systems_with_violations.shp"),
          delete_dsn = TRUE)

## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## NOTES
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## - PWSID prefix filtering (str_starts(PWSID, "IL")) captures Illinois-
##   primacy systems. A small number of tribal systems in Illinois may be
##   coded under an EPA region prefix rather than "IL" -- check EPA_REGION
##   in SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS.csv if tribal systems are in scope.
##
## - COUNTY_SERVED in SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv is self-reported and known to
##   be incomplete/inconsistent (EPA notes this explicitly in the data
##   dictionary). For a jurisdictional map, consider validating this list
##   against a spatial join of the PWSID-linked service area boundaries
##   (from download_water_system_boundaries.R) to the Cook County polygon --
##   the two methods should mostly agree, and discrepancies are worth
##   reporting rather than silently reconciling.
##
## - OWNER_TYPE_CODE decodes as: F = Federal, L = Local government,
##   M = Public/Private, N = Native American, P = Private, S = State.
##   This is your key field for the "who owns/operates" governance dimension
##   -- e.g., flagging municipal (L) vs. investor-owned (P) systems.
##
## - RULE_CODE == "350" isolates Lead and Copper Rule violations specifically
##   (see full rule code list in SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT.csv documentation,
##   captured in this script's data dictionary reference).
##
## - VIOLATION_STATUS categories (Resolved / Archived / Addressed /
##   Unaddressed) are EPA's own compliance framing -- "Unaddressed" and
##   "Addressed" both indicate the violation has not reached a resolving
##   enforcement action, and are treated here as "unresolved" for a simple
##   summary count. Adjust this grouping if your analysis needs the
##   Resolved/Archived distinction preserved (e.g., Archived violations
##   dropped out of active compliance tracking after 5 years regardless of
##   resolution, per EPA's Enforcement Response Policy).
##
## - This is quarterly-snapshot data (SUBMISSIONYEARQUARTER field); the bulk
##   download represents the latest quarter only. For a violations *history*
##   across time, EPA's SDWA_downloads_cy.zip (cumulative year) or the
##   individual violations file's date fields may be needed instead --
##   check https://echo.epa.gov/files/echodownloads/ for current file options.
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

## Lead Service Lines

Lead service line data were obtained from the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency's (IEPA) Service Line Material Inventory Reports [@iepa2025lsl]. Under the Lead Service Line Replacement and Notification Act [@illinois2021], every community water supply in Illinois must submit an annual inventory of the service lines connected to its distribution system, classified by material. IEPA publishes these submissions as a single statewide file containing one record per water system per reporting year (2017–2024). Each record gives the system's total service connections and the number of lines that are lead, galvanized, copper (with or without lead solder), cast or ductile iron or transite, plastic, of unknown material, or of unknown material but known not to be lead. Records are keyed to the system's PWSID, which allows direct linkage to the service area boundaries and SDWIS compliance data described above.

The statewide file was filtered to water systems that IEPA lists as located in Cook County, together with any systems identified as serving Cook County through SDWIS or through the service area boundaries, so that systems listed under a neighboring county but serving Cook County residents were retained. Service line materials were then collapsed into five categories: lead; galvanized; unknown material; non-lead (copper, iron or transite, plastic, and unknown-but-not-lead); and unclassified lines, meaning connections not assigned to any material category. The unclassified category is needed because the reporting form changed over time. Reports for 2024 include only lead and unknown counts, and some 2022 reports do not fully break down the system total. For each system and year, the shares of lines that are lead, of unknown material, and lead, galvanized, or unknown combined (i.e., lines that may require replacement) were calculated relative to total service connections.

Because not all systems report every year, each system's most recent inventory was identified and joined by PWSID to the service area boundaries, with the reporting year retained so that comparisons across systems account for differences in reporting year. These inventories are system-level counts rather than line- or parcel-level locations; they indicate how many lead lines a system has, but not where those lines are within its service area. Counts are self-reported, and large numbers of lines of unknown material reflect incomplete field verification rather than confirmed presence or absence of lead.

```{r}
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Standardize IEPA Service Line Material Inventory Reports for Cook County
## water systems and join each system's most recent inventory to the
## service area boundaries.
##
## Source: Illinois EPA, Lead Service Line Information
## https://epa.illinois.gov/topics/drinking-water/public-water-users/lead-service-line-information.html
## File: ServiceLineMaterialInventoryReports.csv (downloaded manually and
## saved to the data/ folder).
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

library(dplyr)
library(readr)

## ---- 1. Read the statewide inventory file ------------------------------------
## One row per water system (FacilityId = PWSID) per reporting year.

lsl_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/ServiceLineMaterialInventoryReports.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    .default      = col_integer(),
    FacilityId    = col_character(),
    County        = col_character(),
    FacilityName  = col_character(),
    ReportedDate  = col_character(),
    ReportingYear = col_integer()
  )
) |>
  mutate(ReportedDate = as.POSIXct(ReportedDate, format = "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p",
                                   tz = "America/Chicago"))

## ---- 2. Keep Cook County systems ---------------------------------------------
## Systems IEPA lists under Cook County, plus any system identified as
## serving Cook County via SDWIS (cook_pwsids) or the service area
## boundaries (cook_cws), so cross-county systems are not dropped.

lsl_cook_raw <- lsl_raw |>
  filter(County == "Cook" | FacilityId %in% union(cook_pwsids, cook_cws$PWSID))

## ---- 3. Standardize material categories --------------------------------------
## 2024 reports include only lead and unknown counts, and some 2022
## reports are incomplete, so lines not assigned to any category are kept
## as "unclassified" rather than assumed to be non-lead.

cook_lsl_history <- lsl_cook_raw |>
  mutate(
    lsl_total        = TotalServiceConnections,
    lsl_lead         = ServicesLead,
    lsl_galvanized   = ServicesGalvanized,
    lsl_unknown      = ServicesUnknownMaterial,
    lsl_non_lead     = ServicesCopperLeadSolder + ServicesCopperNonLeadSolder +
                       ServicesCastDuctileIronTransite + ServicesPlastic +
                       ServicesUnknownNotLead,
    lsl_unclassified = pmax(lsl_total - (lsl_lead + lsl_galvanized + lsl_unknown + lsl_non_lead), 0L),
    lsl_pct_lead            = if_else(lsl_total > 0, lsl_lead / lsl_total, NA_real_),
    lsl_pct_unknown         = if_else(lsl_total > 0, lsl_unknown / lsl_total, NA_real_),
    lsl_pct_lead_or_unknown = if_else(lsl_total > 0,
                                      (lsl_lead + lsl_galvanized + lsl_unknown) / lsl_total,
                                      NA_real_)
  )

## ---- 4. Most recent inventory per system --------------------------------------

cook_lsl_latest <- cook_lsl_history |>
  group_by(FacilityId) |>
  arrange(desc(ReportingYear), desc(ReportedDate), .by_group = TRUE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  rename(lsl_reporting_year = ReportingYear)

## ---- 5. Join to service areas --------------------------------------------------

cook_cws_with_violations <- cook_cws_with_violations |>
  left_join(
    cook_lsl_latest |>
      select(PWSID = FacilityId, lsl_reporting_year, lsl_total, lsl_lead,
             lsl_galvanized, lsl_unknown, lsl_non_lead, lsl_unclassified,
             lsl_pct_lead, lsl_pct_unknown, lsl_pct_lead_or_unknown),
    by = "PWSID"
  )
```

# Analysis

## Study Scope

This brief focuses on the community water systems serving suburban Cook County, the area within the Cook County Department of Public Health's (CCDPH) jurisdiction. The City of Chicago is outside CCDPH's jurisdiction and is excluded from the primary analysis. Chicago's water system is also a fundamentally different unit from suburban systems. It is a single, large, well-resourced utility serving about 2.75 million people, whereas suburban Cook County's roughly 2.5 million residents are served by more than 140 separate systems ranging from a few dozen to about 83,000 people. Because most Safe Drinking Water Act obligations, and therefore most violations, accrue per system rather than per resident, direct comparisons of violation counts between Chicago and the suburbs largely reflect this difference in structure rather than differences in water quality.

Chicago is nonetheless retained as context. The Chicago Department of Water Management supplies treated Lake Michigan water to most suburban Cook County communities, so its treatment and corrosion control practices shape the water that many suburban residents receive. Chicago's service area is shown on the map below for reference, and a limited comparison using measures that do not depend on system size is provided in [Comparison with the City of Chicago].

Four suburban jurisdictions (Evanston, Oak Park, Skokie, and Stickney Township) are served by their own certified local health departments rather than by CCDPH. Their six water systems (Evanston, Oak Park, Skokie, Stickney, Central Stickney Sanitary District, and South Stickney Sanitary District) are retained in the suburban totals but reported separately where relevant and flagged on the map. They can be excluded from the map by setting `include_independent_hd <- FALSE` in the scope chunk below.

```{r}
#| label: define-study-scope
#| eval: true
#| echo: false

## Water systems outside CCDPH's public health jurisdiction.
chicago_pwsid <- "IL0316000"

independent_hd_pwsids <- c(
  "IL0310810",  # Evanston
  "IL0312250",  # Oak Park
  "IL0312880",  # Skokie
  "IL0313000",  # Stickney (Stickney Township)
  "IL0315570",  # Central Stickney SD (Stickney Township)
  "IL0317370"   # South Stickney SD (Stickney Township)
)

## TRUE keeps the independent health district systems (flagged) in the
## suburban analysis; FALSE drops them.
include_independent_hd <- TRUE

cook_cws_with_violations <- cook_cws_with_violations %>%
  mutate(jurisdiction = case_when(
    PWSID == chicago_pwsid               ~ "City of Chicago",
    PWSID %in% independent_hd_pwsids     ~ "Independent health district",
    TRUE                                 ~ "CCDPH"
  ))

chicago_cws <- cook_cws_with_violations %>%
  filter(jurisdiction == "City of Chicago")

suburban_cws <- cook_cws_with_violations %>%
  filter(jurisdiction != "City of Chicago",
         include_independent_hd | jurisdiction != "Independent health district")
```

## Summary of Suburban Community Water System Service Areas and Violations

<!-- NOTE: The figures in this section were tallied from the
cook_cws_with_violations data frame as produced by
drinking_water_dataprep.qmd from the May 2026 SDWA quarterly snapshot,
and from IEPA's Service Line Material Inventory Reports (latest report
per system). They are static text, not computed at render time, and
should be re-checked whenever the underlying data are refreshed. -->

Excluding Chicago, 165 community water system service areas intersect suburban Cook County. Of these, 142 systems are identified in SDWIS as serving Cook County and therefore carry violation and compliance data. Six of these 142 serve the independent health districts, leaving 136 systems that serve the CCDPH jurisdiction. The remaining 23 service areas belong to systems in neighboring counties (including three in Indiana) whose boundaries touch the county but which do not list Cook County as a county served. The summaries below describe (1) the area and types of service areas, (2) the population and service connections of these systems, and (3) the overall magnitude of drinking water violations. All figures are approximate.

### Service Area Extent and Types

Municipal water systems dominate the suburban landscape, accounting for 130 of the 165 service areas and the large majority of the land area served. The remaining systems are a mix of residential areas served by private utilities (e.g., Aqua Illinois and Illinois American Water), sanitary improvement districts, mobile home parks, wholesale water commissions, homeowners associations, and medical facilities (@tbl-cws-types).

| Service area type | Systems | Approx. area (km²) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Municipality | 130 | ~1,700 |
| Residential Area / Other Residential | 15 | ~157 |
| Sanitary Improvement District | 6 | ~24 |
| Mobile Home Park | 8 | ~2.4 |
| Wholesaler of Water | 2 | ~7 |
| Homeowners Association | 2 | ~1.5 |
| Medical Facility | 2 | ~0.4 |
| **Total** | **165** | **~1,895** |

: Community water system service areas intersecting suburban Cook County, by service area type {#tbl-cws-types}

The 142 suburban systems with SDWIS data cover roughly 1,357 km², of which the CCDPH jurisdiction's 136 systems account for about 1,282 km². Boundary provenance is mixed: 97 boundaries are EPA-modeled estimates, predominantly from a random forest model, while 68 are system-sourced, nearly all of them derived by tracing or buffering municipal lead service line inventories. Only one boundary (Hazel Crest) carries a confirmation date. Nearly all systems are owned by local governments; 19 are privately owned (mobile home parks, homeowners associations, and investor-owned utility systems) and one is federal (Edward Hines Jr. VA Hospital).

### Population and Service Connections

The 142 suburban systems serve roughly 2.5 million people through about 766,000 service connections. The 136 systems in the CCDPH jurisdiction serve about 2.27 million people through about 695,000 connections (@tbl-cws-population).

| Geography | Systems | Population served | Service connections |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Suburban Cook County | 142 | ~2.50 million | ~766,000 |
| CCDPH jurisdiction | 136 | ~2.27 million | ~695,000 |
| Independent health districts | 6 | ~236,000 | ~71,000 |

: Population served and service connections of suburban Cook County community water systems {#tbl-cws-population}

Most systems are mid-sized. Across the 165 suburban service areas, one serves more than 100,000 people (Elgin, which lies mostly in Kane County), 95 serve 10,001–100,000, 31 serve 3,301–10,000, 25 serve 501–3,300, and 13 serve 500 or fewer. The largest systems in the CCDPH jurisdiction include Cicero (83,000), Schaumburg (75,750), Arlington Heights (73,320), Palatine (70,875), and Des Plaines (60,675). Suburban systems average about 3.3 residents per service connection. Population and connection counts in the boundary layer occasionally diverge from those in SDWIS; for example, Evanston lists 28,783 connections in the boundary layer and 14,657 in SDWIS.

### Magnitude of Drinking Water Violations

Across the 142 suburban systems, SDWIS records approximately 8,230 violations, of which about 1,540 (19%) are health-based, about 219 are unresolved, and about 805 (10%) are Lead and Copper Rule violations. Systems in the CCDPH jurisdiction account for nearly all of them (@tbl-cws-violations). Every suburban system but one (Aqua Illinois–Timber Ridge) has at least one recorded violation.

| Geography | Violations | Health-based | Unresolved | Lead and Copper Rule |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Suburban Cook County | ~8,230 | ~1,540 | ~219 | ~805 |
| CCDPH jurisdiction | ~7,920 | ~1,510 | ~212 | ~770 |
| Independent health districts | 309 | 28 | 7 | 35 |

: SDWA violations among suburban Cook County community water systems {#tbl-cws-violations}

Systems in the CCDPH jurisdiction average about 3.5 recorded violations per 1,000 residents served, but violations are concentrated in a relatively small number of systems:

- **Highest total violation counts** are found predominantly in the south suburbs: Sauk Village (689), Ford Heights (580), Bartlett (300), Robbins (271), Phoenix (248), Richton Park (218), Dixmoor (172), Park Forest (161), Lemont (153), and Markham (150).
- **Small systems have the highest per-capita burdens.** Measured per 1,000 residents served, rates reach about 365 for Des Plaines Mobile Home Park, 320 for Ford Heights, 250 for Illinois American–Midwest Palos, 230 for Candlelight Village Mobile Home Park, 228 for Glen Eden Estates Homeowners Association, and 221 for Golf.
- **Groundwater systems are disproportionately affected.** The 16 systems relying on groundwater serve only about 95,000 people (about 4% of the CCDPH jurisdiction's population) but account for roughly 2,000 violations (about a quarter of the jurisdiction's total). Most other systems purchase treated Lake Michigan water.
- **Health-based violations are highly concentrated.** Bartlett alone accounts for 257 health-based violations, followed by Lemont (90) and Blackhawk Estates Mobile Home Park (89).
- **Lead and Copper Rule violations cluster in older inner-ring and south suburban communities**, led by Phoenix (40), Dixmoor (38), Maywood (27), South Holland (27), Ford Heights (21), and Berwyn (19).
- **Unresolved violations** are most numerous in Robbins (15), Summit (10), Dixmoor (9), Calumet Park (9), and Burnham (8).

Taken together, these patterns indicate that drinking water compliance problems in suburban Cook County are concentrated among small, groundwater-dependent, and lower-income south suburban systems, rather than distributed in proportion to population. This finding aligns with the environmental justice concerns described in the [Literature Review].

### Lead Service Line Inventories

According to each system's most recent IEPA Service Line Material Inventory Report [@iepa2025lsl], the systems IEPA lists in the CCDPH jurisdiction report about 686,000 service connections, of which about 107,600 (16%) are lead and about 129,100 (19%) are of unknown material. Counting galvanized lines as well, about 35% of service lines may require replacement. Lead lines are reported by 75 of these 154 systems and are heavily concentrated: Cicero (about 15,200), Des Plaines (11,500), Evergreen Park (6,600), Maywood (5,000), and Calumet City (4,400) together account for nearly 40% of the jurisdiction's known lead lines. The independent health districts report a higher share, with about 30% of lines lead and about 66% lead, galvanized, or unknown. Systems' most recent reports range from 2020 to 2024 (most are from 2022 or 2024), so these figures combine inventories from different years.

### Comparison with the City of Chicago

Counts of SDWA violations are not a meaningful basis for comparing Chicago with suburban Cook County. Chicago records 214 violations, only 2 of them health-based and 4 under the Lead and Copper Rule, but this low count reflects its operation as a single, large system, its high-quality Lake Michigan source, and its dedicated compliance capacity. It does not indicate a lower risk of lead exposure. The Lead and Copper Rule's 90th-percentile compliance test, which Chicago generally meets through long-standing corrosion control treatment, has been criticized for understating lead at the tap.

Lead service line inventories offer a fairer comparison because they are measured per service connection and do not depend on system size (@tbl-lsl-comparison).

| Geography | Service connections | Lead | Unknown material | Lead, galvanized, or unknown |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| City of Chicago (2024) | ~487,000 | ~150,800 (31%) | ~251,600 (52%) | 83% |
| Suburban Cook County | ~743,000 | ~124,400 (17%) | ~149,900 (20%) | 37% |
| CCDPH jurisdiction | ~686,000 | ~107,600 (16%) | ~129,100 (19%) | 35% |
| Independent health districts | ~57,000 | ~16,800 (30%) | ~20,800 (37%) | 66% |

: Lead service line inventories, City of Chicago and suburban Cook County (most recent IEPA report per system) {#tbl-lsl-comparison}

By this measure, Chicago's potential lead service line burden is considerably higher than that of suburban Cook County. More than four in five of its service lines are lead or of unknown material, compared with about one in three in the CCDPH jurisdiction. The large unknown share in Chicago's 2024 report also reflects the new reporting format, which records only lead and unknown counts. A further comparison of the share of residents served by a system with a recent health-based violation would require violation dates restricted to a defined time window (see [Data Limitations]).

### Data Limitations

Several features of the underlying data warrant caution when interpreting these figures:

- **Most recent violation date.** The `most_recent_violation` field is derived from SDWIS's `VIOL_LAST_REPORTED_DATE`, which records when a violation was last *reported*, not when it occurred. Most systems share the same date (2026-05-27 for 107 systems and 2006-12-06 for 15), dates that appear to reflect EPA data refresh and migration events. The field should not be interpreted as the date of the most recent violation.
- **Possible double counting.** Violation counts are drawn from SDWIS's combined violations and enforcement file, which may contain one record per violation–enforcement action pair. If so, violations with multiple enforcement actions are counted more than once.
- **Unmatched systems.** Twenty-three systems whose service areas intersect Cook County (e.g., Elgin, Elmhurst, Barrington, Roselle, Hinsdale, Frankfort, and Illinois American–West Suburban) lack SDWIS data because Cook County is not listed among the counties they serve, even though some do serve Cook County residents.
- **Unclipped boundaries and cross-county systems.** Service areas are retained in full rather than clipped to the county line, so area and population totals for systems that extend beyond Cook County (e.g., Elgin, Bartlett, Barrington, and Orland Park) include territory and residents outside the study area.
- **Implausible modeled boundaries.** Some EPA-modeled boundaries are far smaller than the communities they serve, such as Stone Park (0.016 km² for 4,576 residents), South Stickney Sanitary District (0.2 km² for 30,000 residents), and River Forest (0.66 km² for 11,717 residents). These distort area-based measures such as the violation density shown in the map below.
- **Wholesale systems.** Wholesale water commissions (Justice–Willow Springs and DuPage Water Commission) report populations that overlap with those of the retail systems they supply.
- **Jurisdictional assignment.** Water systems are assigned to the CCDPH jurisdiction or an independent health district by the community they serve; systems whose service areas straddle these boundaries are assigned as a whole.
- **Lead service line inventories.** Inventories are self-reported, system-level counts drawn from different reporting years and formats, and the systems IEPA lists in Cook County (160 suburban systems) do not exactly match the 142 suburban systems with SDWIS data.

## Interactive Map of Community Water System Violations

To support exploration of how SDWA violation burden is distributed across suburban Cook County's community water system service areas, the compliance summary and service area boundaries joined above as `cook_cws_with_violations` (see [Drinking Water Violation and Compliance]) are rendered here as an interactive `leaflet` map, limited to the suburban systems defined in [Study Scope]. Service areas are shaded using quintile-based bins of total violation count (`n_violations`), calculated from suburban systems only so that Chicago does not affect the bin breaks, and so that shading reflects the empirical distribution of violations across systems rather than a fixed, potentially uninformative interval scheme. The City of Chicago's service area is shown in gray for reference only, and systems serving the independent health districts (Evanston, Oak Park, Skokie, and Stickney Township) are outlined with a dark dashed border. The Cook County boundary (`cook_county`) is layered on top as a reference outline. Hovering over a service area surfaces the system's identifying information (name, PWSID, service area type, and public health jurisdiction), scale (population served, service connections), and compliance history (total, health-based, unresolved, and Lead and Copper Rule violation counts, plus the most recent violation date). A violation density measure (violations per square mile, calculated from the boundary layer's `Area_SqKM` field) is also included in the hover panel to help distinguish systems with a genuinely concentrated violation burden from large-area systems that may simply accumulate more violations by virtue of serving more territory.

```{r}
#| label: leaflet-map-cws-violations
#| eval: true
#| out-width: "100%"
#| out-height: "700px"

## ---- 0. Carto basemap API key --------------------------------------------------
## CARTO_API_KEY authenticates the Carto Basemaps raster tile service used for
## the light "Positron" basemap below (see https://basemaps.cartocdn.com).

CARTO_API_KEY <- "cb1_31xh_1_06fb99adb466f0f5a0392d7d"

## ---- 1. Derive violation density (per square mile) --------------------------
## Area_SqKM is the service area's shape-derived area in square kilometers;
## convert to square miles (1 sq km = 0.386102159 sq mi) and divide total
## violations by area. Guard against zero/NA area to avoid Inf/NaN densities
## for slivers or unresolved boundary geometries.

suburban_cws <- suburban_cws %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi = Area_SqKM * 0.386102159,
    violation_density_sqmi = if_else(
      !is.na(area_sqmi) & area_sqmi > 0,
      n_violations / area_sqmi,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

## ---- 2. Quintile bins for total violation count ------------------------------
## Quantile breaks are data-driven (vs. a fixed interval scheme) so shading
## reflects the actual distribution of violations across suburban systems
## (Chicago is excluded; see the define-study-scope chunk).
## Many systems may share the same (often zero) violation count, which can
## collapse some quantile breaks together -- unique() drops any resulting
## duplicate break so colorBin() receives strictly increasing bin edges.

violation_bins <- quantile(
  suburban_cws$n_violations,
  probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2),
  na.rm = TRUE
) %>%
  unique()

violation_pal <- colorBin(
  palette = "viridis",
  domain = suburban_cws$n_violations,
  na.color = "transparent",
  bins = violation_bins,
  reverse = TRUE
)

## ---- 3. Hover labels ----------------------------------------------------------

cws_labels <- sprintf(
  "<strong>%s</strong><br/>
  PWS ID: %s<br/>
  Service area type: %s<br/>
  Public health jurisdiction: %s<br/>
  Population served: %s<br/>
  Service connections: %s<br/>
  Violations (total): %s<br/>
  Health-based violations: %s<br/>
  Unresolved violations: %s<br/>
  Lead and Copper Rule violations: %s<br/>
  Most recent violation: %s<br/>
  Violation density (per sq mi): %s",
  suburban_cws$PWS_Name,
  suburban_cws$PWSID,
  suburban_cws$Service_Area_Type,
  suburban_cws$jurisdiction,
  format(suburban_cws$Population_Served_Count, big.mark = ","),
  format(suburban_cws$Service_Connections_Count, big.mark = ","),
  format(suburban_cws$n_violations, big.mark = ","),
  format(suburban_cws$n_health_based, big.mark = ","),
  format(suburban_cws$n_unresolved, big.mark = ","),
  format(suburban_cws$n_lead_copper_rule, big.mark = ","),
  as.character(suburban_cws$most_recent_violation),
  formatC(suburban_cws$violation_density_sqmi, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
) %>%
  lapply(htmltools::HTML)

## Independent health district systems get a dark dashed border; all
## others keep the default thin white border.
is_independent_hd <- suburban_cws$jurisdiction == "Independent health district"
cws_border_color  <- if_else(is_independent_hd, "#333333", "white")
cws_border_weight <- if_else(is_independent_hd, 2, 0.5)
cws_border_dash   <- if_else(is_independent_hd, "6 4", "3")

chicago_label <- htmltools::HTML(paste0(
  "<strong>City of Chicago</strong><br/>",
  "Outside CCDPH jurisdiction; shown for reference only.<br/>",
  "Population served: ", format(chicago_cws$Population_Served_Count, big.mark = ",")
))

## ---- 4. Build the interactive map ---------------------------------------------

CARTO_API_KEY <- "cb1_31xh_1_06fb99adb466f0f5a0392d7d"

leaflet(width = "100%", height = 700) %>%
  addTiles(
    urlTemplate = paste0(
      "https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/rastertiles/light_all/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=",
      CARTO_API_KEY
    ),
    group = "Positron (minimal)"
  ) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldImagery, group = "World Imagery (satellite)") %>%
  addPolygons(
    data = chicago_cws %>% st_transform(crs = 4326),
    group = "City of Chicago (reference)",
    fillColor = "#BDBDBD",
    fillOpacity = 0.5,
    weight = 1,
    opacity = 0.8,
    color = "#808080",
    label = chicago_label,
    labelOptions = labelOptions(
      style = list("font-weight" = "normal", padding = "3px 8px"),
      textsize = "13px",
      direction = "auto"
    )
  ) %>%
  addPolygons(
    data = suburban_cws %>% st_transform(crs = 4326),
    group = "Water System Violations",
    fillColor = ~violation_pal(n_violations),
    weight = cws_border_weight,
    opacity = 0.8,
    color = cws_border_color,
    dashArray = cws_border_dash,
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    highlight = highlightOptions(
      weight = 3,
      color = "#666",
      dashArray = "",
      fillOpacity = 1,
      bringToFront = TRUE
    ),
    label = cws_labels,
    labelOptions = labelOptions(
      style = list("font-weight" = "normal", padding = "3px 8px"),
      textsize = "13px",
      direction = "auto"
    )
  ) %>%
  addPolylines(
    data = cook_county %>% st_transform(crs = 4326),
    stroke = TRUE,
    weight = 2.5,
    opacity = 1,
    fillOpacity = 0,
    color = "black",
    group = "Cook County Boundary"
  ) %>%
  addLegend(
    "bottomleft",
    pal = violation_pal,
    values = suburban_cws$n_violations,
    title = "SDWA Violations, suburban<br>systems (count, quintile bins)",
    opacity = 1
  ) %>%
  addScaleBar(position = "bottomright") %>%
  addFullscreenControl() %>%
  addResetMapButton() %>%
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Positron (minimal)", "World Imagery (satellite)"),
    overlayGroups = c("Water System Violations", "City of Chicago (reference)",
                      "Cook County Boundary"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  )
```
